analysis.one_liner: Strengthens protections for employees who report securities fraud, including ending forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a single vote despite sponsorship from two Republicans and three Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand protections for people who report securities fraud to the SEC. Employees who report misconduct internally to a supervisor would gain protection from retaliation, people accused of retaliating could no longer keep the case away from a jury, and employers could no longer force workers to sign away their right to sue before a dispute arises. It would also require the SEC to decide whistleblower award claims on a set timeline instead of leaving them open-ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of banks, broker-dealers, investment advisers, and other SEC-regulated firms who report securities violations gain new protections: reporting to a supervisor or other company authority would count as protected activity, retaliation claims could go to a jury, and predispute arbitration clauses could no longer force those disputes into private arbitration. Whistleblowers waiting on SEC award decisions would get a required decision timeline, with extensions only after written notice. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Extends anti-retaliation protection to workers who report suspected securities violations internally — to a supervisor or a colleague believed to have authority to investigate or stop the misconduct — instead of only to the SEC, and covers pre- and post-employment retaliation.
Gives either side in an anti-retaliation case the right to a jury trial, so an employer can no longer have a judge decide the case alone.

Makes predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for whistleblower disputes and bars waiving the law's rights and remedies, meaning a worker cannot be forced to sign away these protections as a condition of employment.

Requires the SEC to make an initial decision on a whistleblower award claim within one year of the filing deadline or one year after related litigation ends, with any extension requiring written notice to the whistleblower.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms and public companies regulated by the SEC would bear the cost: broader retaliation liability that now reaches internal reports, jury trials in retaliation cases, the loss of forced arbitration for whistleblower disputes, and pressure to resolve award claims faster. Some of that cost would come as increased litigation and compliance expenses.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face materially more litigation exposure: internal reports to supervisors become protected activity, retaliation cases go to juries, and forced arbitration is off the table, which raises the cost of resolving workplace disputes and, critics argue, invites weak or opportunistic claims.

The 'prompt payment' mandate is softer than it looks: the Enforcement Director can extend the deadline by 180 days for complexity or multiple whistleblowers, and repeat extensions are possible with Commission approval, so slow award decisions could continue.
Both the jury-trial and arbitration changes apply retroactively to claims already pending when the bill would take effect, changing the rules for disputes already underway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are well targeted: workers who see securities fraud are the people best positioned to report it, and the bill closes real gaps (internal reporting was excluded after a 2018 Supreme Court decision, and forced arbitration quietly neutralized many claims). The main honest cost falls on regulated firms in the form of litigation risk, and the award-timing mandate contains enough exceptions that it may not deliver the promised speed. On balance a modest, fairly designed bill — which makes its quiet death in committee more notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on March 31, 2022, joined from the start by Senators Warren, Collins, Warnock, and Cortez Masto — two Republicans and three Democrats.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day; that was the last action of any kind.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, broker-dealers, investment advisers, and other SEC-regulated employers are better off because the bill died: they avoid broader retaliation liability, jury trials in whistleblower cases, and the ban on forced arbitration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that avoid new whistleblower liability

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — two Republicans (Grassley, Collins) and three Democrats (Warren, Warnock, Cortez Masto) — and no vote was ever taken, so the parties' positions were never tested.

industries.note: These SEC-regulated firms would face retaliation suits from employees who reported misconduct internally, and could no longer enforce predispute arbitration clauses against whistleblowers. Their interest in avoiding this liability runs directly against the workers and investors the protections serve.

Executives and boards of SEC-registered companies would lose a layer of insulation: internal whistleblowers gain protection, retaliation cases can reach a jury, and existing arbitration agreements covering these disputes become unenforceable.

The bill removes predispute arbitration as the default forum for securities whistleblower disputes, shifting those cases to court. Firms that relied on private, non-jury resolution of these claims lose that tool.
